hints: Think about what kind of reagent $\text{OH}^{-}$ is and which carbon in G it will attack, look at the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond polarity.
Remember where each curly arrow must start and finish, one from the nucleophile and one from the bond that breaks.
walkthrough:
Spot the nucleophile and electrophile**
Picture $\text{OH}^{-}$ with its full negative charge and lone pairs. It is electron rich and loves electron poor centres. In $\text{C-Cl}$, chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, so carbon is $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and chlorine is $\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$. That $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ is your target.

Draw the attack and the leaving group leaving**
Start a curly arrow on a lone pair on O and point it straight to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$. At the same time the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond must break. Draw a second curly arrow from the middle of the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond onto Cl to give $\text{Cl}^{-}$. That pair of arrows is nucleophilic substitution to form prenol.

Final answer: Curly arrow from lone pair on O of $\text{OH}^{-}$ to C of $\text{C-Cl}$.
$\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown with curly arrow from $\text{C-Cl}$ bond to $\text{Cl}$.

hints: Steam adds $\text{H}$ and $\text{OH}$ across the $\text{C=C}$ in prenol, consider Markovnikov addition to give two possible diols, then use the oxidation result to pick J.
walkthrough:
Use the negative tests to identify J**
Prenol plus steam gives diols of formula $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{2}$. Heating J with excess acidified dichromate gives a product that does NOT react with 2,4-DNPH, so no aldehyde or ketone is formed. That means J must contain only alcohol groups that resist oxidation, a tertiary alcohol plus a primary alcohol that somehow is not oxidised to a carbonyl here, the key isomer is the one with a tertiary $\text{OH}$ at the Markovnikov position: $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.

Final answer: J is $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, displayed as $\text{H}_{3}\text{C}-\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{CH}_{3})-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.

hints: K and L share the same connectivity but are stereoisomers and both oxidise to the same product M containing a carbonyl, think which diol has one secondary and one primary $\text{OH}$.
walkthrough:
Find the only other diol connectivity**
The other addition of water across the double bond puts $\text{OH}$ on the less substituted carbon, giving $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. This has a chiral centre at $\text{CH}(\text{OH})$, so it exists as a pair of stereoisomers. Both oxidise with excess dichromate to the same keto acid M, which fits the 2,4-DNPH positive result.
Final answer: K and L are $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.

hints: K and L have the same structural formula but are non superimposable mirror images due to a carbon with four different groups.
walkthrough:
Link chirality to the isomer type**
Look at $\text{CH}(\text{OH})$ in $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. It is bonded to H, OH, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}$, four different groups. That chiral centre gives a pair of enantiomers, which is optical isomerism.
Final answer: Optical isomerism.

hints: Count atoms in K, $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{2}$, and M, $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{3}$, and balance the extra O and H using [O] and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Balance with [O] as oxidant**
K has two $\text{OH}$ groups, one primary oxidised to carboxylic acid (needs 2[O]) and one secondary oxidised to ketone (needs 1[O]), total 3[O]. Add $2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ on the right to balance H and O: $$\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{2} + 3[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{3} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Recall the classic room temperature addition reaction that distinguishes alkenes from alkanes by a clear colour change.
walkthrough:
Choose the addition test**
Alkenes decolourise bromine water by electrophilic addition across $\text{C=C}$ to form a colourless dibromo compound. Shake prenol with orange $\text{Br}_{2}(\text{aq})$ and the orange colour disappears, confirming the alkene.
Final answer: Add bromine water, $\text{Br}_{2}(\text{aq})$, turns from orange to colourless.

hints: Addition polymerisation opens the $\text{C=C}$ to a $\text{C-C}$ single bond, keep all other groups unchanged and show the continuation bonds.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond**
Take prenol $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C=CHCH}_{2}\text{OH}$ and convert $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{C-C}$. The two carbons each gain one continuation bond. So you get $$-\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH})-$$ with brackets and an n, showing one repeat unit of poly(prenol).
Final answer: Repeat unit: $-\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH})-$

hints: Find the longest chain containing the $\text{OH}$ group in N and number to give $\text{OH}$ the lowest number.
walkthrough:
Name the primary alcohol**
N is $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. The longest chain with $\text{OH}$ has 4 carbons with $\text{OH}$ on C1 and a methyl branch on C3, so 3-methylbutan-1-ol.

hints: Compare the physical state of Ni (solid) with isoprenol (liquid) and hydrogen (gas) in reaction 1.
walkthrough:
Check the phases**
Ni is a solid while the reactants are liquid and gas, so catalyst is in a different phase from reactants. That is heterogeneous catalysis.
Final answer: Heterogeneous

hints: P is a carboxylic acid and it reacts with ethanol under acid to form what functional group, think sweet smell.
Draw the carbon skeleton without showing C and H labels and then recall why sweet smelling esters are useful commercially.
walkthrough:
Form the ester**
P is $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ reacting with $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$ with $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ under reflux. That is esterification, acid plus alcohol gives ester plus water. So Q is the ethyl ester: $$\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{COOC}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$$ Draw it skeletal, zig zag chains with $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-O}$ clearly shown.

Recall why esters matter**
Sweet smelling liquids like this are classic fruity esters. They are widely used as flavourings, perfumes or solvents, any one of these earns the mark.

Final answer: Q is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ (ethyl 3-methylbutanoate) shown as skeletal formula.
Commercial use: solvents or perfumes or flavourings.

hints: Reaction I consumes the alkene, so look for the bond that disappears as the $\text{C=C}$ is lost.
walkthrough:
Track the disappearing bond**
Reaction I converts $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$ to a chloroalkane, so the $\text{C=C}$ stretch disappears. Monitor the absorption at $1500-1680$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ for $\text{C=C}$, its loss shows reaction progress.
Final answer: $\text{C=C}$ at $1500-1680$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$

hints: Reaction II extends the carbon chain by one carbon to form $\text{C-C}\equiv\text{N}$, what cyanide nucleophile does this.
walkthrough:
Supply the cyanide source**
Changing $\text{R-Cl}$ to $\text{R-C}\equiv\text{N}$ is nucleophilic substitution by $\text{CN}^{-}$. Use ethanolic $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$, heated, to provide the nucleophile.
Final answer: Potassium cyanide, $\text{KCN}$ (or sodium cyanide, $\text{NaCN}$).

hints: Reaction III converts $\text{R-C}\equiv\text{N}$ to $\text{R-COOH}$ using $\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, name this bond breaking by water.
walkthrough:
Name the nitrile to acid change**
Breaking the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ with hot aqueous acid to give a carboxylic acid is hydrolysis, here acidic hydrolysis.
Final answer: (Acidic) hydrolysis

hints: Reaction I is electrophilic addition of HCl to an alkene via a carbocation, compare the carbocation formed here with a more substituted alternative.
Think about how alkyl groups donate electron density to a positive centre and how the number of alkyl groups differs.
walkthrough:
Identify the unstable intermediate**
HCl addition to this alkene can give a primary $1^{\circ}$ carbocation. Primary carbocations are much less stable than tertiary $3^{\circ}$ ones, so the activation energy is high and the pathway is slow, giving very low yield of that product.

Explain with the inductive effect**
Alkyl groups push electron density toward the positive carbon, the positive inductive (+I) effect, spreading and stabilising the charge. With only one alkyl group attached instead of three, the +I stabilisation is much smaller, so the $1^{\circ}$ cation is high in energy and forms slowly.

Final answer: Reaction I proceeds via a less stable $1^{\circ}$ carbocation intermediate (compared to a $3^{\circ}$ carbocation).
Fewer alkyl groups give a smaller positive inductive (+I) effect, so less stabilisation of the positive charge.
